findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Previously agrred Service Efficiencies & Income Proposals 2026-27
findings.headline: Garden waste fees to increase progressively to £67 by 2027/28, well below neighboring councils' charges
findings.detail: Building on an already-agreed increase from £49 to £59 in 2026/27, the council proposes further increases to £67 in 2027/28 with potential for gradual future increases. Service levels (25 collections per year) remain unchanged. Neighboring councils charge £70 (Vale of White Horse), £75 (South Oxfordshire), and £94 (Oxford City).
findings.matters: Progressive fee increases show the council is managing service sustainability through charges. The gap to neighboring councils (£67 vs £75-£94) suggests either deliberate under-pricing or demand resistance, creating income risk if take-up does not meet targets.
findings.quote: Increase garden waste fees to keep Cherwell's garden waste service sustainable and broadly aligned with neighbouring districts – providing an increase in income of £0.203m in 2027/28 and £0.228m in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Previously agrred Service Efficiencies & Income Proposals 2026-27
findings.headline: Three-weekly waste collection proposal targets £0.265m saving despite uncertain commitment status
findings.detail: The council proposes moving to three-weekly collection cycles for residual waste, stated to cut landfill by 14% and boost recycling. The proposal is described as to 'explore' this change, yet appears in the formal MTFS as a 'New Saving' with a specific £0.265m value in 2027/28. This language creates uncertainty about whether the service change is actually committed or still under consideration.
findings.matters: This is a material and potentially contentious service change. If public or political resistance prevents implementation, the £0.265m shortfall would need to be covered elsewhere. Lenders need to know whether this is firm policy or exploratory.
findings.quote: Explore moving to a three-weekly green bin collection to cut landfill by 14%, boost recycling and capture more food waste - providing a saving of £0.265m in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Previously agrred Service Efficiencies & Income Proposals 2026-27
findings.headline: Banbury Museum transition creates £0.178m MTFS savings dependent on securing external funding
findings.detail: The council is supporting the Banbury Museum to transition to alternative funding sources and reduce council grant dependency from 2027/28 onwards. Savings build from £0.028m in 2027/28 to £0.050m per year from 2028/29 onwards. Success requires the museum to secure external funding; failure would likely require council backfill or service reduction.
findings.matters: Material savings targets depend on an external organization's ability to find alternative funding. This creates contingent liability risk: if the museum cannot secure external support, the council must choose between backfilling or reducing the service.
findings.quote: Support Banbury Museum to transition to a new operating model of sustainable funding sources by 2027/28, reducing its dependency on council grant funding and building a more resilient, community-driven institution - providing a saving of £0.028m in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Previously agrred Service Efficiencies & Income Proposals 2026-27
findings.headline: Council treasury and investment income strategy contributes £0.5m to 2026/27 budget but does not recur
findings.detail: The council plans to optimize cash flow and investment strategies to generate higher interest income of £0.5m in 2026/27 only. This material single-year benefit does not appear in future MTFS years. The document does not specify whether this is from higher interest rates, improved cash positioning, or expected investment returns.
findings.matters: Investment income is volatile and sensitive to interest rate and market changes. A one-off £0.5m dependency in a single year represents a specific budget risk if rates fall or cannot be sustained.
findings.quote: Continue to optimise cash flow and investment strategies through effective treasury management, resulting in higher interest income. This additional revenue will be retained to support the council's general operations - providing a benefit of £0.500m in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Previously agrred Service Efficiencies & Income Proposals 2026-27
findings.headline: Pension fund valuation improvement supports £1.0m MTFS savings
findings.detail: The council has negotiated revised employer pension contributions based on an improved pension fund valuation. This generates £0.500m savings in 2026/27, £0.250m in 2027/28, and £0.250m in 2028/29. The document does not explain the source of the improvement or whether it represents a sustained change in contribution rates.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are typically one of a council's largest balance-sheet items. An improved valuation and lower contribution rates reduce budget pressure and improve financial position, but lenders need to know if this is one-off or sustainable.
findings.quote: Agree revised employer pension contributions based on the improved valuation of the council pension fund -providing a saving of £0.500m in 2026/27, £0.250m in 2027/28 and £0.250m in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Commercial waste demand growing at 17% per year, requiring new IT system
findings.detail: Commercial waste demand is growing at approximately 17% per year, requiring investment in a new IT system to manage demand. This growth rate far exceeds typical service demand and suggests either significant business opportunity or mounting cost pressures.
findings.matters: Growth at 17% annually is material and could indicate either revenue opportunity or escalating costs depending on cost structure and pricing model
findings.figures: circa 17% per year
findings.quote: Implement an IT system to effectively manage the demand on the waste management service which is growing by circa 17% per year

findings.headline: Software and licensing costs of £0.050m emerging as prior funding sources cease
findings.detail: Computer software and licensing costs of £0.050m now require core budget funding because 'other sources are no longer available'. This indicates a prior funding stream (departmental budget or external funding) has ended, pushing costs into the main budget.
findings.matters: Loss of prior funding sources signals emerging structural cost pressures mounting from multiple directions across the council
findings.quote: Fund computer software and licensing costs previously not included in the core budget as other sources are no longer available – requiring £0.050m in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Housing benefits overpayment income falling £0.050m as claimants move to universal credit
findings.detail: The council faces structural income loss of £0.050m due to housing benefit claimants transferring to universal credit. This ongoing decline reflects national welfare policy changes beyond the council's control.
findings.matters: This is a continuing structural income loss that will persist as more claimants transition to universal credit, representing a permanent erosion of council resources
findings.quote: Fund the reduced grant income received by the council of £0.050m as housing benefit claimants transfer to universal credit.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs of £0.500m ongoing despite acknowledged need to reduce
findings.detail: The council continues funding nightly charged accommodation at £0.500m in 2026/27. While costs have reduced year on year, the council explicitly identifies this as 'an area that the council is looking to reduce through the provision of more cost-effective solutions', signalling this remains an unresolved budget problem.
findings.matters: High ongoing costs combined with stated intent to reduce suggests management challenge; failure to find more cost-effective solutions will sustain this budget pressure
findings.quote: Continue to fund nightly charged accommodation – requiring investment of £0.500m in 2026/ 27. Note that the cost of this provision has reduced year on year and continues to be an area that the council is looking to reduce through the provision of more cost-effective solutions.

findings.headline: Court costs income falling £0.150m due to strategic shift away from court recovery
findings.detail: The council is changing its council tax recovery approach to agree payment arrangements before pursuing court action. This deliberate policy shift results in a material loss of £0.150m in court costs income in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A permanent £0.150m reduction in council income without an offsetting saving places significant pressure on the budget and reduces funds available to service debt
findings.quote: Fund the strategic change in approach to agree council tax recovery options before court action is required, resulting in less court cost income of £0.150m.

Combined £5m commitment to temporary housing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Programme as at June 2026
findings.headline: PSDS4 decarbonisation scheme: Woodgreen Leisure Centre works cancelled; council increasing match funding by £210k to preserve scheme elsewhere
findings.detail: Works at Woodgreen Leisure Centre cannot be delivered in a way that meets the grant conditions and are being cancelled with no grant claim. To compensate, the council has increased its match funding by £210k to deliver works at other sites (Stratfield Brake, North Oxford Academy, Spiceball LC).

findings.quote: Detailed design and feasibility confirmed proposed works at Woodgreen Leisure Centre could not be delivered in a way that meets grant conditions. These works are not proceeding and there will be no expenditure or grant claim for these. CDC 26/27 match funding is increased by £210k

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Programme as at June 2026
findings.headline: Transforming Market Square Bicester: major regeneration project in validation phase expecting material cost increases
findings.detail: This major regeneration project is now in a validation stage to test deliverability, particularly highways impacts. The council explicitly states that based on latest information there will likely be an increase in overall project costs, with a report to follow to Executive.
findings.matters: A large capital scheme (£5.9m forecast) is entering a critical phase with cost pressures now expected, requiring Executive approval of revised budgets before spending accelerates.
findings.figures: Transforming Market Square (40286); budget £5,049k; forecast £5,941k; cost increase expected
findings.quote: Following the evolution of the preferred design, a validation stage is being undertaken to test deliverability, particularly in relation to highways, before progressing to the next phase of design. findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Programme as at June 2026
findings.headline: Thorpe Lane Depot: £46k cost increase plus additional £382k Gate 0 required to complete electrical renewal
findings.detail: Substation installation costs have increased by £46k beyond original estimate. Additionally, an extra £382k Gate 0 has been submitted to complete the full project scope, indicating the total cost is materially higher than originally budgeted.
findings.matters: Demonstrates significant cost increases on a routine infrastructure renewal, suggesting either underestimation at procurement or scope creep requiring additional approvals and funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Programme as at June 2026
findings.headline: Kidlington Leisure Centre hit by grid capacity constraint: council seeking DNO reimbursement for previously paid sums
findings.detail: The council has been advised there is insufficient electricity supply available from the DNO for the planned sub-station at Kidlington Leisure Centre. This external constraint has forced modification of leisure centre controls to run ASHPs to manage the shortfall. The council is now seeking reimbursement from the DNO for previously paid grant sums.
findings.matters: This represents a hard infrastructure constraint imposed by the grid operator that is outside the council's control and requires negotiation with the DNO for recovery of previously committed funds.
findings.figures: Kidlington Leisure New Electrical Main (40263); budget £200k; insufficient grid capacity for sub-station
findings.quote: Due to electrical network capacity issues, we have been advised there is insufficient electricity supply available for the planned sub-station. CDC are seeking reimbursement from DNO of previously paid grant sums.

findings.headline: Funding 'cliff-edge' risk at 2029/30 when transitional support arrangements end, creating major uncertainty in the tail of the MTFS.
findings.detail: The council identifies a cliff-edge in 2029/30 when transitional funding arrangements are expected to cease, with 'major uncertainty' about how this will be handled. The funding advisors flag this as the single largest uncertainty beyond the core period, suggesting potential for significant, abrupt reductions in resources.
findings.matters: This signals risk of a step-change funding reduction at 2029/30 that could force emergency savings or reserve drawdown, affecting the council's financial stability in year 3 of the MTFS.
findings.figures: Cliff-edge risk materializes 2029/30; next funding review expected 2029/30
findings.quote: The major uncertainty is likely to be how transitional support is handled, with many authorities currently sitting on a cliff-edge at the end of 2029/30.

findings.headline: Pay award and contract inflation assumptions revised upward from 2.5%/2% to 3.5%/3%, increasing the cost base across the entire MTFS period.
findings.detail: The updated MTFS increases assumed pay awards by one percentage point to 3.5% and contract inflation by one percentage point to 3%, both applied across all years to 2031/32. These revisions indicate that actual cost pressures are running ahead of previous forecasts and must be offset by deeper savings or income growth.
findings.matters: Upward revisions to inflation assumptions reveal that cost forecasts are already proving insufficient, reducing confidence in the savings plan's adequacy.
findings.figures: Pay awards 2.5%→3.5%; contract inflation 2%→3%
findings.quote: It will assume 3.5 percent pay awards over the MTFS period. Contract inflation will be provided for at 3 percent in all years of the MTFS.

findings.headline: Unitary Authority merger with West Oxfordshire effective April 2028 has no transition costs built into the MTFS despite an earmarked reserve being set aside.
findings.detail: The council will merge into a new unitary authority in year 2 of the current MTFS (1 April 2028). While an earmarked reserve has been created for disaggregation and creation costs, the paper explicitly states that no financial assumptions have been modeled for this transition period, creating material unbudgeted cost risk.
findings.matters: A major structural reorganization with unquantified costs occurring mid-MTFS creates uncertainty about whether the reserve will be adequate and whether additional borrowing will be needed.
findings.figures: Merger effective 1 April 2028 (year 2 of 5-year MTFS to 2031/32)
findings.quote: From 1 April 2028, Cherwell and West Oxfordshire will be combined into a new Unitary Authority (UA). At this point, no assumptions have been built into the MTFS in relation to the transition period before the new UA is 'stood up'.

findings.headline: Cherwell faces £2.335m savings requirement in 2027/28 with explicit acknowledgment that 2026/27 savings non-delivery will increase the gap further.
findings.detail: The MTFS identified £2.335m in annual savings needed for 2027/28. The council is actively monitoring £2.290m of savings planned for 2026/27 and explicitly flags that if these fail to deliver on an ongoing basis, the 2027/28 gap will widen. This signals material risk of a larger, unplanned savings requirement.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the council can execute savings plans; non-delivery signals increasing reliance on reserves or further cuts to essential services.
findings.figures: £2.335m required for 2027/28; £2.290m being monitored in 2026/27
findings.quote: To the extent that savings anticipated in 2026/27 are not delivered on an ongoing basis this will increase the level of savings required in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Non-domestic rates write-offs of £0.098m add to collection pressure on a second key revenue stream
findings.detail: The council is writing off £0.026m via S151 Delegation and £0.072m via Committee approval for business rates in 2026/27. Combined with council tax write-offs, total debt write-offs across council tax, business rates, and sundry debts reach £0.426m for the year.
findings.matters: Business rates collection volatility compounds budget predictability risk; tracking this alongside council tax write-offs indicates whether collection difficulty is spreading across multiple revenue streams.
findings.figures: £0.098m non-domestic rates write-offs in 2026/27; £0.426m total write-offs across all debt categories
findings.quote: Non-Domestic Rates to be written off under S151 Delegation in July 2026 0.026 Non-Domestic Rates written off via Committee Approval 0.072

findings.headline: £0.236m of council tax debts written off in 2026/27, concentrated in collection difficulties
findings.detail: Cherwell is writing off £0.171m under S151 Delegation and £0.063m via Committee approval for council tax collection. The council maintains a bad debt provision of £0.767m described as sufficient, and the provision is reviewed regularly. No indication in the paper whether this is increasing or stable versus prior years.
findings.matters: Council tax is a primary revenue source; write-offs of this scale indicate collection difficulties that affect budget stability and cash flow predictability, which matters to lenders assessing resilience.
findings.figures: £0.236m total council tax write-offs in 2026/27; £0.767m bad debt provision
findings.quote: Council Tax due to be written off under S151 Delegation in July 2026 0.171 Council Tax to be written off via Committee  0.063 Total write offs in financial year 2026/2027 0.236

findings.matters: Income forecasting variance of this scale suggests the assumptions underlying the service plan may be unreliable, a concern for future budget predictability.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Detailed Narrative on Forecast June 2026
findings.headline: Regeneration & Economy has limited further mitigation capacity despite £0.033m overspend
findings.detail: Regeneration & Economy is forecasting £0.033m overspend due to costs associated with devolution, staffing changes, and Future Oxford Partnership. The paper notes that in-year budget mitigations have already been committed, leaving very limited scope for further mitigation.
findings.matters: When a service explicitly states mitigations are exhausted and more money is being spent than budgeted, the council has limited room to absorb further pressures or unexpected costs in that area.
findings.figures: £0.033m overspend; limited mitigation headroom
findings.quote: In-year budget mitigations have already been committed, leaving very limited scope for further mitigation. These costs will be retained within the directorate.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Detailed Narrative on Forecast June 2026
findings.headline: Environmental Services agency staffing costs of £0.290m are the main cost driver and require ongoing management
findings.detail: Agency staffing is forecast at £0.290m and is identified as the principal driver of Environmental Services overspend. While partially offset by vacant posts and savings elsewhere, the council continues to closely monitor and seek to mitigate these costs throughout the year.
findings.matters: Persistent high agency costs suggest difficulty recruiting or retaining permanent staff, and such pressures tend to be sticky and difficult to reverse mid-year.
findings.figures: £0.290m agency costs forecast; net overspend £0.167m after offsets
findings.quote: The main driver of the overspend is agency costs currently forecast at £290k. This is offset by vacant posts to bring the net cost down to £0.167m

findings.headline: Unfunded WESP partnership commitment of £0.070m was approved in 2025 but missed from budget
findings.detail: Environmental Services committed to an additional £0.070m contribution for the WESP partnership this financial year. This was agreed in 2025 but not included in the budget forecast, representing an unfunded expansion of the budget that the service must now cover through reductions elsewhere.
findings.matters: This indicates budget discipline and planning processes that failed to capture an agreed commitment, meaning actual costs exceed planned ones and the council must find mitigations mid-year.
findings.figures: £0.070m unfunded contribution
findings.quote: An additional £0.070m contribution has been agreed for CDC's continued working with the WESP partnership for this financial year. This was agreed in 2025 but missed from budget forecasts so represents an unfunded expansion of the budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Detailed Narrative on Forecast June 2026
findings.headline: Major planning application fee income at significant risk due to Planning Inspectorate designation
findings.detail: Cherwell's £0.224m savings target depends on major planning application fee income, but the council's designation allows applicants to submit major applications directly to Planning Inspectorate, bypassing the council and losing fee income. The paper explicitly warns: there is a significant risk this saving will not be achieved.
findings.matters: An unachievable £0.224m saving directly reduces the council's financial capacity and suggests income forecasting assumptions may have been optimistic or based on assumptions that have since changed.
findings.figures: £0.224m planning application fee income saving at risk
findings.quote: the Council's designation, applicants can submit major applications directly to Planning Inspectorate (PINS), resulting in the loss of fee income to the Council therefore resulting to the saving as being non deliverable. Until there is greater certainty regarding the duration of designation and the pipeline of major applications, there remains a significant risk that the full £224k saving will not be achieved in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Executive Finance Performance & Risk Monitoring Q1 Report
findings.headline: New high-risk entry added to Corporate Risk Register: Planning Applications for Major Development scored as Very High
findings.detail: A new risk (C05A) has been added to the Corporate Risk Register during Q1 and is rated as Very High impact and Very Likely (likelihood 5). The report does not explain the specific drivers of this risk in the main text, but it appears in the context of sustained planning performance challenges and the Local Plan examination delays.
findings.matters: A Very High risk on major planning applications signals the council recognises it cannot currently process or approve major development. For a lender, this is a red flag: without the ability to approve major schemes, developer activity will collapse, reducing s106 income, increasing council reliance on borrowing, and signalling governance stress.
findings.figures: C05A - Planning Applications for Major Development rated Very High
findings.quote: One new risk has been added to the Corporate Risk Register C05A Planning Applications for Major Development.

findings.paper_title: Executive Finance Performance & Risk Monitoring Q1 Report
findings.headline: Planning function is severely stressed: only 38.7% of non-major applications meet the national processing target, and the council was recently placed into national Designation for poor major application performance
findings.detail: The council is reporting 38.7% of non-major planning applications determined on time against a national indicator target of 70% or more. On major applications, 11.2% are being overturned at appeal against a 10% target, which triggered MHCLG placing the council into Designation. Although the council reports improvements have been made and it is now below the MHCLG 10% target, the overall performance picture shows a planning function under significant strain.
findings.matters: Planning delays kill development viability and damage developer confidence in the council. Given the 50% housing delivery shortfall, planning performance matters directly to economic recovery. A lender would worry about statutory intervention and whether the council can recover without external support.
findings.figures: Non-major applications: 38.7% on time vs 70% target. Major application appeal overturn rate: 11.2% vs 10% target
findings.quote: % of Non-Major Planning Applications determined to National Indicator: Reporting 38.7% against a target of 70% or more. The planning improvement work we are delivering will be seeking to reduce this and improve the response time for processing applications.

findings.paper_title: Executive Finance Performance & Risk Monitoring Q1 Report
findings.headline: Capital programme is in overspend and major regeneration project is being reprofiled due to forecast overrun
findings.detail: The full capital programme (all years) is forecast to spend £42.733m against a budget of £42.089m—a £0.644m overspend. Place & Regeneration alone accounts for £0.660m overspend. The Transforming Market Square Bicester project (£5.049m) is being reprofiled and £0.370m moved out of 2026/27 to future years 'due to the project needing to consider the best way forward considering forecast overspend.' This suggests the project cost is rising and timescale is slipping.
findings.matters: Capital overspends and reprofiling signal project management weakness and escalating costs. For a lender, this raises questions about the council's ability to deliver major schemes on time and on budget, and whether prudential borrowing will be wasted or stretched.
findings.figures: Total capital budget £42.089m; forecast spend £42.733m; overspend £0.644m. Place & Regeneration overspend £0.660m. Transforming Market Square Bicester: £0.370m reprofiled out of 2026/27
findings.quote: Transforming Market Square Bicester 5.049 (0.370) 1.181 Reprofiling due to the project needing to consider the best way forward considering forecast overspend.

findings.paper_title: Executive Finance Performance & Risk Monitoring Q1 Report
findings.headline: Housing delivery is running 50% behind target, affecting local economic growth and developer confidence
findings.detail: The council delivered 790 new dwellings in 2026/27 against a target of 1,582—a 50% shortfall. The report identifies economic pressures, higher interest rates, global uncertainty, and infrastructure constraints in Bicester and Kidlington as causes. The council has developed a Housing Delivery Action Plan and is working with Homes England, but the gap is large and structural.
findings.matters: Housing shortfall signals economic stress and reduced local activity. For a lender, this means reduced council tax base growth, delayed developer activity that funds infrastructure contributions, and pressure on local services from stalled housebuilding.
findings.figures: 790 dwellings delivered; 1,582 target; shortfall of 792 dwellings (50%)
findings.quote: Result: The end of year 2026/27 figure was 790 dwellings against a target of 1,582 dwellings. Housing delivery continues to be influenced by a range of national and local challenges, including economic pressures, higher interest rates, global uncertainty and ongoing changes to the planning system. Locally, progress in areas such as Bicester and Kidlington has been affected by significant infrastructure constraints.

findings.paper_title: Executive Finance Performance & Risk Monitoring Q1 Report
findings.headline: Planned savings worth £0.449m are not being delivered
findings.detail: The council identified £0.449m of non-delivery against previously approved savings. Environmental Services is not collecting charges for lost/damaged bins (£0.102m) or closing public conveniences at Pioneer Square (£0.026m). Place & Regeneration is not achieving a planned car parking charge increase (£0.050m) and the major one: central government's household application fee change introduced in April 2025 is generating £0.224m less income than budgeted. These are not new pressures—they are planned savings failing to land.
findings.matters: A council that cannot deliver approved savings has a structural budget problem. It is currently in underspend only because interest rates are higher than forecast (£0.249m gain), which is non-recurring. When interest rates normalise, this council has a £0.449m hole to fill.
findings.figures: £0.449m total savings non-delivery; interest rate gain of £0.249m masking the shortfall; without the interest rate benefit, the council would be in a £0.174m overspend position
findings.quote: Savings non-delivery as detailed above relate to: Environmental Services – Charge for lost/ damaged containers - £0.102m; Environmental Services – Transfer/ closure of public conveniences – Pioneer Square - £0.026m; Place & Regeneration - Increase annual car parking charge of no more than 10p per hour - £0.050m; Place & Regeneration - Continue the operation of national changes made to the household applications fee (introduced in April 2025 by central government) – £0.224m.

findings.headline: Five-year housing land supply is only 3.1 years; housing delivery remains below targets
findings.detail: As of the 2025 Annual Monitoring Report approved December 2025, Cherwell has only a 3.1-year housing land supply, well below the statutory 5-year requirement. Despite having over 10,000 homes with planning permission, the district continues to miss housing delivery targets. This makes the council vulnerable to planning by appeal.
findings.matters: Failure to maintain a 5-year housing supply weakens the council's ability to control development and can result in unwanted housing decisions. This also reflects broader economic issues with developer delivery. A lender would see this as indicating developer confidence issues or infrastructure constraints.
findings.figures: 3.1-year housing land supply (2025 AMR); over 10,000 homes with outline or detailed planning permission
findings.quote: It was reported that the district has a 3.1-year housing land supply.

findings.headline: Emergency planning capability gap: training given but not validated; additional resources needed
findings.detail: The emergency planning risk score increased from Low (6) to Moderate (9) in Q1 2026/27. The register notes that attempts to conduct an in-house exercise during 2026 have been unsuccessful due to competing operational demands on staff time. Training has been provided to duty directors and response staff but has never been validated through exercising. A report to the Corporate Leadership Team identified need for additional resource and recommended that strategic response roles be staffed only by Executive Directors and above.
findings.matters: A council unable to exercise its emergency response capability or validate training creates liability and reputational risk. This is not a routine administrative gap; it reflects resource constraint and operational stress. A major incident during this gap would expose both the council and any lender.
findings.figures: Risk score increased from 6 to 9; emergency planning due for review and refresh in 2026
findings.quote: Efforts to deliver an in-house exercise during 2026 have been unsuccessful due to competing operational demands on staff time, resulting in an increased risk position as training has been provided but has not yet been validated through exercising.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation outcome unknown; significant transition costs already set aside
findings.detail: The council is awaiting announcement of a reorganisation decision (devolution/unitarization of local government in Oxfordshire). It has no clarity on the financial impact. The council has already set aside funds to cover transition costs, indicating material exposure. A system-wide SRO and interim Programme Director are in place.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisation could fundamentally change the council's structure, financial position, and service delivery. The council has also set aside an 'interest rate risk reserve' because 'if interest rates do not fall in line with forecasts...then it has set aside an interest rate risk reserve as a further mitigation'.
findings.matters: The council's debt burden is significant and rising as a proportion of its assets. Nearly a third of gross revenue funding goes to servicing debt. Interest rate assumptions are critical to affordability, and the council is preparing for the risk that rates don't fall as forecast. This constrains future borrowing capacity and leaves the council exposed to interest rate volatility.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Corporate Plan Report 2026-27 to Council
findings.headline: Government changed the business rates pooling calculation after consultation, reducing the council's medium-term improvement from £4.4m to £2.1m.
findings.detail: The council had planned on the basis of provisional government guidance, expecting a £4.4m improvement from changes to business rates pooling treatment. When the final settlement was announced on 9 February 2026, the government changed the methodology for calculating pooling income, cutting the expected benefit by nearly half to £2.1m. The council explicitly states this 'severely impacted the council's medium term financial strategy', and it has set aside the one-off Adjustment Support Grant to absorb this shock.
findings.matters: The council's external funding has become less predictable. Government policy changes between provisional and final settlement created a £2.3m negative surprise. This shows reliance on government funding decisions that can shift, with limited notice.
findings.figures: Expected £4.4m improvement reduced to £2.1m; difference of £2.3m
findings.quote: However, the final settlement announced on 9 February 2026 contained materially different funding figures from 2027/28 onwards due to a significant change in the methodology to calculate pooling income. These reduced a £4.4m improvement to £2.1m and have severely impacted the council's medium term financial strategy.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Corporate Plan Report 2026-27 to Council
findings.headline: A £2.3m one-off government grant masks a structural funding deficit that will reappear in 2027-28.
findings.detail: The final government settlement announced on 9 February 2026 included a one-off Adjustment Support Grant of £2.335m to Cherwell for 2026-27, which covers the exact gap that will emerge in 2027-28 when it drops out. The council's MTFS (Table 4.6.2) shows a £2.335m funding gap in 2027-28, with the grant specified as covering 'a late shift from 100% to 50% business rates pooling benefit'. Without the grant, the council would run a deficit in 2026-27.
findings.matters: The council's balance in 2026-27 depends entirely on a non-recurring grant. A lender assessing the council's structural financial position needs to understand that 2026-27 is not a sustainable budget without this one-off support, and that a material funding pressure emerges immediately in 2027-28.
findings.figures: £2.335m Adjustment Support Grant in 2026/27; £2.335m funding gap in 2027/28
findings.quote: The impact on the baseline position is £2.335m, which will be mitigated in 2026/27 by the one-off Adjustment Support Grant, but which will result in an ongoing pressure from 2027/28.

findings.headline: Projects reserve completely depleted to zero by April 2026 after S151 review adds £3.46m
findings.detail: The Projects reserve opened at £5.61m, received £2.15m in transfers during 2025/26, and the S151 officer added a further £3.46m, bringing it to exactly £0.00 by April 2026. This means all project commitments are now accounted for and funded. No project contingency remains.
findings.matters: Once a projects reserve is depleted, any cost overruns on capital schemes or new project needs must be funded from general balances or additional borrowing. Lenders need to know how the council will absorb project pressures.

This signals the council has committed to a substantial transformation or restructuring programme funded from reserves.
findings.matters: Large transformation programmes carry execution risk and can distract senior management. A lender should understand the scope (redundancy, systems, structural) and whether the reserve is adequately funded or whether mid-programme additional funding might be needed.

findings.detail: After drawing only £0.67m during 2025/26, the council forecasts a material £2.27m draw in 2026/27 from its Business Rates Equalisation reserve. This is then topped up slightly (£0.20m per year) but never recovers to current levels. The pattern suggests business rates income is expected to be volatile and pressured in the near term.
findings.matters: Business rates are a volatile revenue stream. A large draw from this reserve signals the council is hedging against a sharp shortfall in 2026/27, which could indicate expected economic weakness or local property market stress.

findings.detail: The Market Risk reserve is forecast to grow from £8.90m to £9.27m in 2025/26, then drawn at escalating rates (£0.59m to £1.00m per year). By 2031 it reaches £12.98m. This reserve exists to absorb unexpected financial volatility, suggesting the council has material exposure to markets (treasury, investments, or market-linked income).
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has treasury or market exposure that could crystallise losses, and whether reserve levels are adequate to absorb shocks without triggering borrowing.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Transitional protection grant of £8.5m in 2028/29 is at risk of removal in 2029/30
findings.detail: The council benefits from £8.5m of transitional protection grant in 2028/29 as a buffer against the business rates reset and Fair Funding 2.0 changes. However, this protection ends after 2028/29, and there is no certainty beyond the current three-year spending review period (to March 2029). While the minister has stated the Government will look to avoid 'cliff-edges,' there is explicit risk this £8.5m is removed from 2029/30.
findings.matters: The £8.5m protection masks a deeper structural funding problem. If removed, it becomes an additional pressure on top of the already-identified £2.3m gap in 2027/28 and any further savings that have not been delivered. This creates potential for a cumulative funding shortfall of over £10m in 2029/30.

findings.headline: Contingency budget reduced, requiring services to identify mitigations with documented service impacts
findings.detail: The corporate contingency budget has been reduced for 2026/27 to £2.2m (5.5% of net budget). This means services projecting overspends must now develop written mitigation plans with explicit service impact statements, rather than drawing from a larger central buffer. The paper states services must 'identify mitigations along with service impacts for the Executive to consider.'
findings.matters: Reduced contingency limits the council's ability to absorb in-year pressures without service cuts or reserve drawdown. Combined with the declining savings delivery rate and rising overspends, this tightening creates higher refinancing risk if the council needs to draw on reserves.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Extreme dependency on business rates and council tax income, both in upper quartile risk
findings.detail: Business rates income represents 302.73% of baseline funding growth (6th highest retained growth of all councils), placing Cherwell in upper quartile risk. Council tax is 51.74% of net expenditure (upper quartile risk) due to nine years of no increases pre-2019. Both streams are volatile to economic and market conditions. The council holds a £9.3m market risk reserve and £5.9m interest rate equalisation reserve specifically for these risks.
findings.matters: The council's revenue model is heavily exposed to factors outside its control: business rates to economic growth and the Government's business rates reset decisions; council tax to property band growth and taxpayer resistance. A downturn in either stream creates immediate budget stress given the emerging 2027/28 gap.
findings.figures: Business rates growth ratio 302.73%; Council tax 51.74% of net revenue expenditure; £9.3m market risk reserve; £5.9m interest rate equalisation reserve held

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Services forecast to overspend by £2.5m in 2025/26, masked by corporate underspend
findings.detail: The 2025/26 forecast as of December 2025 shows £2.499m in service overspends, only offset by £3.024m in corporate underspends, arriving at a balanced outturn. This pattern shows services are not controlling spend to budget. The paper introduces a 2% variance tolerance and Budget Oversight Group for services exceeding this threshold.
findings.matters: Services overspending and relying on central corporate reserves to balance is not a sustainable pattern. It signals weak individual budget control and means corporate reserves are being drawn down in-year rather than held for genuine emergency or investment.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Debt:income ratio of 151% is extreme outlier — six times the district council median
findings.detail: Cherwell holds £165m gross external debt (forecast to fall to £149m by March 2026) against a median debt:income ratio of 9% for district councils. Cherwell's ratio is 151%. This reflects large capital schemes including Castle Quay and Graven Hill financed through borrowing. The council must refinance approximately £41m of maturing debt in 2026/27 at current market rates.
findings.matters: This leverage is extreme for a district council. While the paper claims borrowing costs are 'factored into the budget,' the refinancing risk is real: if interest rates fall more slowly than forecast (or rise), or if service income declines, debt serviceability becomes constrained. The council is also at the upper end of its Authorised Limit for External Debt.
findings.figures: £149m debt forecast March 2026; Cherwell debt:income 151% vs median 9%; ~£41m refinancing needed 2026/27; Authorised Limit £270m (down from £310m in 2025/26)
findings.quote: Cherwell at £165m and in the upper quartile of non-metropolitan district councils. This reflects the decisions taken to finance the capital programme, including Castle Quay and Graven Hill, through borrowing.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Track record of delivering planned savings has deteriorated to 63-66%
findings.detail: Over six years, the council's savings delivery has declined: 80% in 2021/22, 75% in 2022/23, 80% in 2023/24, 63% in 2024/25, and 66% in 2025/26 (forecast). The paper acknowledges this pattern and states that 'where a service is overspending it should identify mitigations.' With £4.1m of savings required through 2030/31 and the emerging £2.3m gap, this deteriorating track record is material.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on a council to deliver cost reduction targets if two-thirds is the recent delivery rate. This limits the council's options for bridging the 2027/28 funding gap and increases refinancing risk.
findings.quote: The council identified a savings programme of £1.7m for 2024/25. The savings delivery was 63% with mitigations identified for non-delivery.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Government settlement change in February 2026 created a £2.3m funding gap from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The final local government finance settlement announced on 9 February 2026 reduced resources by £2.3m from 2027/28 compared to the provisional settlement announced 17 December 2025. The 2026/27 budget is balanced but there is now an identified £2.3m gap in 2027/28 with no funding solution yet identified. The paper states the council must 'identify how it intends to address' this gap.
findings.matters: This is a material structural deficit emerging just 12 months ahead. At £2.3m, it represents a significant portion of the council's discretionary spending. The council has a recent track record of delivering only 63-66% of identified savings targets, raising questions about its ability to close this gap through service reductions.
findings.figures: £2.3m annual reduction from 2027/28 onwards; gap identified for 2027/28, 2029/30, and 2030/31
findings.quote: The final settlement reduced the amount of resources the council will receive by £2.3m from 2027/28. The council now needs to deliver what is planned in the MTFS and identify how it intends to address the £2.3m gap in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Auditor has disclaimed opinion on accounts for three consecutive years
findings.detail: Cherwell received a disclaimed audit opinion for 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25. The paper notes this is a sector phenomenon but the impact is that auditors have not been able to certify the council's accounts. The auditors are developing a roadmap to return to standard opinions. However, the council did receive an unqualified value for money conclusion for both 2023/24 and 2024/25.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not form any opinion on whether the accounts are materially correct. This is a significant governance red flag for external stakeholders and lenders assessing financial position, even if the VfM conclusion is positive.
findings.quote: As a result of receiving a disclaimed audit opinion in 2022/23, the council received a disclaimed opinion for its 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts. These disclaimed opinions are as a result of the 2022/23 disclaimed opinion as the auditors ran out of time to get assurance over the opening balances

findings.headline: Property portfolio is illiquid and cannot be quickly converted to cash in stressed market conditions, limiting ability to refinance debt
findings.detail: The council holds major property assets in retail (Castle Quay, Pioneer Square) and industrial/warehouse (Tramway Industrial Estate) sectors. The strategy acknowledges that 'property is relatively difficult to sell to convert to cash at short notice and can take a considerable period to sell in certain market conditions.' The council recognises 'illiquidity as a risk in property' and notes that whilst the portfolio is uncharged (not pledged as collateral), this 'can expose an owner to greater risk of selling an illiquid asset at an inopportune time' if borrowing becomes unavailable.
findings.matters: If PWLB refinancing became constrained (as it was during COVID), the council might need to liquidate property to repay debt. Selling illiquid retail properties in a weak market would likely require steep discounts, crystallising losses and further eroding the CFR-to-asset cushion.
findings.figures: Castle Quay Centre and Waterfront (Banbury), Pioneer Square (Bicester), Tramway Industrial Estate (Banbury) are the largest strategic assets. Current book value of these four assets: £50.9m.

findings.headline: £5m capital investment in temporary accommodation in 2026/27 signals housing pressure or homelessness crisis management
findings.detail: The council is proposing £3m for purchase of temporary accommodation units and £2m for self-contained temporary accommodation units in Bicester, totalling £5m of the £8.5m capital additions for 2026/27. This suggests either statutory homelessness duty pressures or a deliberate strategy to manage accommodation costs. Such spending indicates underlying demand pressures in the housing/homelessness space that are not being met by existing supply.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation purchases often indicate that service demand (homelessness) is outpacing supply or that existing temporary accommodation spend (usually revenue) is becoming unaffordable, requiring capitalisation. This can be a leading indicator of broader social pressure and future budget stress.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increasing to £238.8m in 2026/27, with CFR now 84% of the council's long-term asset base
findings.detail: The council's CFR (the amount of capital expenditure not yet permanently financed) is forecast to rise from £233.9m in 2025/26 to £238.8m in 2026/27 before declining. More concerning, the ratio of CFR to long-term assets is now 84%, meaning the council's debt is equivalent to 84% of its total capital asset value. This ratio has climbed from 75% in 2020/21, a four-year deterioration. The council projects CFR clearance by 2066 'mainly due to the annual minimum revenue provision' but that is 40 years away.
findings.matters: A rising CFR-to-asset ratio signals that the council is borrowing closer to the limit of its asset base. If further asset valuations fall (as property has done), the cushion shrinks further. A lender wants to see headroom here; at 84%, there is little.
findings.quote: As of 31st March 2025, the Council's CFR amounted to 84 percent of the value of its total capital worth (Long-term asset value), demonstrating that the Council's total capital worth exceeds its borrowing requirement.

findings.headline: Council holds £57m in loans to subsidiaries (Graven Hill, Crown House) with £17m in undrawn commitments and credit loss allowance of £0.7m
findings.detail: The council has advanced £57.2m in loans to subsidiaries, has a loss allowance of £0.7m (indicating recognised credit risk), and is contractually committed to lend a further £17m to Graven Hill. The council notes it recognizes 'loss allowance for loans, reflecting the likelihood of non-payment' and that subsidiaries are assessed individually through full business cases. Repayment depends on the subsidiaries' performance in property development and residential letting markets.
findings.matters: Subsidiary loan defaults would immediately impact the council's cash position and would likely trigger additional MRP charges if loan valuations had to be written down further, creating a direct hit to revenue. The undrawn £17m commitment is a contingent liability that could be drawn if the subsidiary faces construction overruns or market headwinds.
findings.figures: Service loans to subsidiaries: £56.6m gross, £0.6m loss allowance, £56.0m net (2024/25). Commitments to lend: £17.0m to Graven Hill (revolving credit facility to 2026). Bonds and guarantees: £1.4m in place, £10.3m agreed in principle.
findings.quote: Accounting standards (IFRS 9) require the council to set aside loss allowance for loans, reflecting the likelihood of non-payment.

findings.headline: Council's affordability critically depends on income from stressed property holdings that generated only 0.9% return in 2024/25
findings.detail: Service investment income (primarily rental income from properties and loan interest from subsidiaries) represents 29-32% of the council's net revenue stream. This income is essential to offset financing costs; without it, the net financing burden would be unsustainable. However, property investments returned only 0.9% in 2024/25 and are forecast at 0.1% in 2025/26. The document acknowledges the risk explicitly: 'Investment income represents a significant proportion of the net revenue stream and therefore the risks around loss of this income should be monitored closely.'
findings.matters: If tenant default, void rates, or further valuations losses impact rental income, the council could face sudden revenue shortfalls. The council is already operating on a knife edge: the affordability ratio (financing costs minus investment income) is -1.0% for 2026/27 but turns positive (0.9%) by 2028/29, meaning costs start to exceed income.
findings.quote: Investment income represents a significant proportion of the net revenue stream and therefore the risks around loss of this income should be monitored closely.

findings.headline: Strategic property assets have lost £106m in book value, with town-centre retail portfolio under sustained pressure
findings.detail: Four major property investments show cumulative book losses of £106m from their original investment cost. Castle Quay Waterfront lost £45.8m (from £68.6m invested), Castle Quay Shopping Centre lost £56.9m (from £64.7m invested), and Pioneer Square lost £2.9m (from £8.2m invested). The document attributes this to 'the changing nature of town centres and the retail market nationwide' and flags over-exposure to town centre retailing as a specific risk.
findings.matters: A lender's security position depends on asset valuations. Sustained property losses in retail signal either that the council paid too much, market fundamentals have shifted unfavourably, or both. The trend suggests further pressure is possible.
findings.figures: Castle Quay Waterfront: investment £68.6m, book value £22.8m (loss £45.8m); Castle Quay Shopping Centre: investment £64.7m, book value £13.6m (loss £56.9m); Tramway Industrial Estate: investment £9.6m, book value £9.2m; Pioneer Square: investment £8.2m, book value £5.3m (loss £2.9m)
findings.quote: The decline in book values have been driven by multiple factors, particularly the changing nature of town centres and the retail market nationwide.

findings.headline: Financing cost ratio rising to nearly 32% of revenue by 2028/29, driven by declining government grants
findings.detail: The council's ratio of financing costs (interest and MRP) to net revenue stream is forecast to reach 31.9% by 2028/29, up from 28.3% in 2024/25. The document explicitly states 'This indicator shows that the ratio of financing costs to net revenue streams is high and increasing across the MTFS, which is primarily due to the forecast in reduction in revenue resources.' This ratio is trending sharply upward over the five-year forecast.
findings.matters: A lender needs to see headroom in a council's budget for debt service; 32% is at the upper end of prudent levels and leaves little buffer for revenue pressures or service demand shocks.
findings.quote: This indicator shows that the ratio of financing costs to net revenue streams is high and increasing across the MTFS, which is primarily due to the forecast in reduction in revenue resources.

findings.headline: Debt rescheduling opportunity rejected due to higher refinancing costs outweighing discount
findings.detail: PWLB offered a £9.4m discount for early repayment of the council's loans, but refinancing at current market rates (4.45%) exceeds the council's average loan rate of 2.34% by a substantial margin. After amortising the discount over ten years, the net effect would be a £924,383 annual revenue cost—making the opportunity economically unfeasible.
findings.matters: The council's inability to execute debt restructuring despite a material discount reflects the structural cost of rising refinancing rates. This constrains the council's financial management options and signals higher debt servicing costs ahead.
findings.figures: Available discount: £9,373,131; Amortised annual discount: £937,313; Increased annual interest cost at 4.45%: £1,861,695; Net annual revenue burden: £924,383; Council's average loan rate: 2.34%
findings.quote: In September 2025 the PWLB was offering a discount of £9,373,131 for the early repayment of all the loans made to the council that have over 12 months left to maturity... Currently the PWLB 1 year rate is 4.45% which would mean an increased interest payments of £1,861,695 annually, reduced by the £937,313 amortised discount, would be an increased revenue burden of £924,383.

findings.headline: Investment cash portfolio declining alongside rising refinancing costs
findings.detail: The council's liquid investment portfolio is forecast to fall from £26m in 2025/26 to £23m in 2026/27, reducing expected investment income from £0.886m to £0.826m. This contraction occurs as the council finances its capital programme through internal borrowing—drawing down reserves rather than accessing external debt.
findings.matters: Shrinking cash reserves combined with lower investment income reduces the council's financial flexibility and its ability to self-finance capital projects or absorb unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Investment portfolio: £26m (2025/26) to £23m (2026/27); Investment income: £0.886m (2025/26 budget) to £0.826m (2026/27 budget); Average interest rate: 3.38% to 3.54%
findings.quote: The budget for treasury investment income in 2026/27 is £0.826m, based on an average investment portfolio of £23m at an average interest rate of 3.54%. This is a slight decrease from the £0.886m budgeted for in 2025/26, based on an average investment portfolio of £26m

findings.headline: Capital reserves forecast to decline by 72% in a single year
findings.detail: Capital reserves are projected to fall from £4.7m in 2025/26 to £1.3m in 2026/27, a loss of £3.4m. This sharp depletion represents a significant erosion of the council's capital resource buffer in just twelve months, with reserves remaining at that low level in subsequent forecasts.
findings.matters: A rapid drawdown of capital reserves signals either heavy capital spending or a deteriorating liquidity position. Either indicates reduced financial resilience and capacity to absorb future shocks.
findings.figures: Capital Reserves: £5.3m (2024/25 actual), £4.7m (2025/26 forecast), £1.3m (2026/27 forecast), £1.2m (2027/28 forecast), £1.2m (2028/29 forecast)

findings.headline: £1m of savings over three years (2026/27 to 2028/29) based on pension fund valuation gains that may not be durable
findings.detail: The council proposes reducing employer pension contributions based on 'improved valuation of the council pension fund,' planning to take £0.500m in 2026/27, then £0.250m in each of 2027/28 and 2028/29. This assumes pension valuations remain improved; if the fund underperforms at the next triennial valuation, these savings would need to be reversed.
findings.matters: £1m of three-year savings dependent on pension fund valuation gains creates structural budget risk; adverse market conditions could force rapid reversal of these cuts.
findings.quote: Agree revised employer pension contributions based on the improved valuation of the council pension fund -providing a saving of £0.500m in 2026/27, £0.250m in 2027/28 and £0.250m in 2028/29.

findings.headline: £0.500m treasury management income planned for 2026/27 depends on sustained elevated interest rates; assumes no material rate decline
findings.detail: Proposal 27 includes 'higher interest income' from optimised treasury and investment strategies generating £0.500m in 2026/27 to support general operations and strategic objectives. This assumes interest rates remain elevated; any material decline in rates would erode this income assumption.
findings.matters: A £0.500m annual income assumption dependent on the interest rate environment creates budget fragility; declining rates would force equivalent cuts or alternative funding sources.
findings.figures: £0.500m benefit 2026/27; 92% public support for proposal
findings.quote: Continue to optimise cash flow and investment strategies through effective treasury management, resulting in higher interest income. This additional revenue will be retained to support the council's general operations and contribute to the delivery of its strategic objectives - providing a benefit of £0.500m in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Capital investment of £3m (2026/27) and £2m (2027/28) for temporary accommodation depends on government funding described as 'could be made available', not confirmed
findings.detail: The council proposes acquiring and constructing temporary accommodation to prevent homelessness with combined investment of £5m. Both proposals state 'the government has indicated that there could be funding made available to contribute towards temporary accommodation projects.' The conditional language ('could') indicates funding is not yet committed, creating delivery and borrowing risk.
findings.matters: £5m of capital investment dependent on unconfirmed external government funding creates borrowing, cash flow, and delivery risk if funding does not materialise as anticipated.
findings.figures: £3m 2026/27 + £2m 2027/28; 75% and 69% public support respectively
findings.quote: To strengthen our efforts in preventing homelessness, we will look to acquire property that will serve as temporary accommodation for individuals and families in need. To achieve this, we are proposing an investment of £3m for 2026/27. The government has indicated that there could be funding mad e available to contribute towards temporary accommodation projects.

findings.headline: Three-weekly waste collection has only 40% support with specific concerns about hygiene, vermin, and fly-tipping creating operational and reputational risk
findings.detail: Moving to three-weekly residual waste collection received only 40% support with 60% opposed. The consultation explicitly notes 'concerns include hygiene, vermin, and fly tipping, issues that carry high reputational and operational risk.' The council recommends consideration of 'seasonal models, enhanced comms, or capacity adjustments' rather than proceeding as proposed.
findings.matters: A household-facing service cut with 60% opposition and documented concerns about service degradation (hygiene, vermin, fly-tipping) presents significant execution risk and potential reputational damage to council credibility.
findings.figures: 40% support, 60% opposition; proposed saving of £0.265m in 2027/28
findings.quote: Explore moving to a three -weekly green bin collection to cut landfill by 14%, boost recycling and capture more food waste - providing a saving of £0.265m in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Banbury Museum grant reduction faces only 29% public support following co-ordinated campaign opposition, creating implementation risk for £0.258m planned saving
findings.detail: The proposal to reduce council grant funding to Banbury Museum by £0.258m (saving in 2027/28) received only 29% support versus 71% opposition. The consultation explicitly notes it was 'strongly opposed following an externally co-ordinated campaign' with residents emphasising culture, education, and local heritage. The council's own recommendation acknowledges this requires 'further engagement and analysis' and suggests exploring alternatives to 'abrupt cuts.'
findings.matters: A budgeted savings of £0.258m in 2027/28 with 71% public opposition and acknowledged need for further engagement has substantial execution risk and may not materialise, creating a budget hole.
findings.figures: 29% support, 71% opposition; £0.258m saving planned for 2027/28
findings.quote: Support Banbury Museum to transition to a new operating model of sustainable funding sources by 2027/28, reducing its dependency on council grant funding and building a more resilient, community-driven institution - providing a saving of £0.258m in 2027/28.
